original_question: A hypersurface M of S^(n+1) is called a Dupin hypersurface when the multiplicities of its principal curvatures are constant and each principal curvature is constant along its principal directions. Determine when such a Dupin hypersurface is of finite type, and determine when a finite type Dupin hypersurface of a hypersphere must be isoparametric.
target_in_paper: Problem 4 in Section 4.2: "When is a Dupin hypersurface of a hypersphere to be of finite type? When is a finite type Dupin hypersurface of a hypersphere to be isoparametric?"
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's target very closely. It correctly singles out Dupin hypersurfaces in S^{n+1}, uses essentially the same Dupin condition stated in Section 4.2, and preserves the official two-part structure of Problem 4: first characterize when such hypersurfaces are of finite type, and second characterize when finite-type Dupin hypersurfaces of a hypersphere are isoparametric.
missing_details: In this paper, 'finite type' is the Euclidean finite-type notion from Section 2.1: for the inclusion x: M -> S^{n+1} ⊂ E^{n+2}, the position vector must admit a finite spectral decomposition x = c + x_1 + ... + x_k with Δx_i = λ_i x_i.
The operator Δ is the Laplace-Beltrami operator of the induced metric on M; this is implicit in the draft but explicit in Section 2.1.
To be fully stand-alone, the ambient space should be stated as a hypersphere S^{n+1} sitting in Euclidean space E^{n+2}, since the finite-type definition is made in Euclidean space.
The official problem is a characterization question ('When is ...?'), not the unconditional assertion that every finite-type Dupin hypersurface must be isoparametric.

No extra hypotheses such as compactness, mass-symmetry, or an upper bound on the number of distinct principal curvatures belong to Problem 4 itself, even though nearby text mentions a partial result for compact Dupin hypersurfaces with at most three distinct principal curvatures.
For a fully self-contained version, 'isoparametric' should be spelled out in the paper's sense for hypersurfaces of a sphere: having constant principal curvatures.
refined_question: Let x: M -> S^{n+1} ⊂ E^{n+2} be a Dupin hypersurface, meaning that the multiplicities of its principal curvatures are constant and each principal curvature is constant along its corresponding principal directions. Determine precisely when M is of finite type in the sense of Chen, i.e. when the Euclidean position vector of the inclusion admits a finite Laplace-Beltrami spectral decomposition x = c + x_1 + ... + x_k with Δx_i = λ_i x_i, and determine precisely when a finite-type Dupin hypersurface of a hypersphere must be isoparametric, that is, have constant principal curvatures.
justification: The draft is targeting Section 4.2, not the broader neighboring Problem 3 on all finite-type hypersurfaces of a hypersphere. Section 4.2 first defines a Dupin hypersurface and then states Problem 4 in essentially the same two-part wording as your draft. To make the question genuinely stand-alone and faithful to the paper, one must import the paper's Euclidean spectral definition of finite type from Section 2.1 and the paper's spherical definition of isoparametric from Section 2.5. Section 4.1 supplies the nearby context that finite-type spherical hypersurfaces are being studied via their Euclidean inclusion, and that isoparametric hypersurfaces form a distinguished subclass in this discussion.
